headline_result_summary: In cross-sectional OLS regressions across the 500 largest US community water systems in 2015, private (investor) ownership (Private sector = 1, n = 58 vs. public [government + cooperative] = 0, n = 442) is associated with significantly higher annual household water bills (+$144.04/year, p < 0.01; unadjusted $501 vs. $315) and a higher percentage of income spent on water by lowest-quintile households (+1.55 percentage points, p < 0.01; unadjusted 4.39% vs. 2.84%), indicating worse household water affordability under private ownership (or equivalently, better affordability under public ownership). State regulatory environments favorable to private investors (NJ and PA) are associated with +$88.64 higher annual water bills (p < 0.01) but have no statistically significant association with lowest-quintile income share (+0.46, p >= 0.05), while state PUC regulation of public utilities has no statistically significant association with either annual bills (36.43) or low-income affordability (0.29).
specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Outcome polarity (sign-to-valence trap): Both outcomes—Annual water bill ($) and Percent of household income spent on water services by the lowest income quintile (%)—measure cost/burden where HIGHER numerical values mean WORSE affordability ('less affordability'). Positive raw coefficients (+144.04** and +1.55** for Private sector; +88.64** for Favorable private regulation) therefore correspond to UNFAVORABLE affordability impacts, not improved access. 2. Public vs. private pole symmetry: The regressions code Private sector = 1 (investor-owned, n = 58) vs. 0 = public (combining 321 government-owned and 121 cooperative utilities). Under the authors' coded exposure (privatization / private ownership), the valence is unfavorable_to_access; if a synthesis instead frames the exposure as public ownership (as discussed on p. 9: 'public ownership is related to lower prices'), the valence flips to favorable_to_access. 3. Regulatory heterogeneity across outcomes: 'Favorable private regulation (1 = NJ, PA)' is purely a two-state indicator (not a nationwide statutory measure) and is statistically significant for annual water bill (+88.64**) but null for low-income income share (0.46, p >= 0.05); meanwhile 'PUC regulates public utilities' is null on both outcomes (all 58 private utilities in the sample were already PUC-regulated, so private PUC regulation could not be estimated). 4. PDF font-encoding / missing minus signs in Tables 1-3: The PDF text layer omits minus signs on negative numbers (e.g., Table 2 prints Groundwater as 46.97** and 0.52** and Service population (ln) as 10.96 and 0.20*, whereas prose on pp. 8-9 confirms negative signs/lower bills; Table 2 footnote also prints '**p , 0.0' for p < 0.01, and standard errors/t-stats are omitted). Positive signs on Private sector (+144.04**, +1.55**) and Favorable private regulation (+88.64**) are explicitly verified by the prose ('$144 higher', '1.55% more', '$89 higher'). 5. Simulated standardized bills: Affordability is computed from rate schedules for a fixed 60,000 gal/year indoor consumption divided by city/county ACS lowest-quintile income, excluding wastewater/stormwater charges and household-level assistance program discounts or actual shutoff rates.
study_design: Cross-sectional observational study using ordinary least squares (OLS) multivariate regressions and descriptive group comparisons (2015 tariff and 2011-2015 ACS data)
unit_and_sample_size: Community water systems matched to city/county socioeconomic data; N = 500 largest community water systems in the US (across 321 counties in 48 states and DC, collectively serving ~140 million people; 58 investor-owned private systems and 442 public systems [321 government-owned, 121 cooperative])
